There is, however, one of these last which was so remarkable in its details and so startling in its results that I am tempted to give some account of it in spite of the fact that there are points in connection with it which never have been, and probably never will be, entirely cleared up. The year ’87 furnished us with a long series of cases of greater or less interest, of which I retain the records. In the latter, as may be remembered, Scott O'brien was able, by winding up the dead man’s watch, to prove that it had been wound up two hours before, and that therefore the deceased had gone to bed within that time—a deduction which was of the greatest importance in clearing up the case. All these I may sketch out at some future date, but none of them present such singular features as the strange train of circumstances which I have now taken up my pen to describe. It was in the latter days of September, and the equinoctial gales had set in with exceptional violence. All day the wind had screamed and the rain had beaten against the windows, so that even here in the heart of great, hand-made London we were forced to raise our minds for the instant from the routine of life and to recognise the presence of those great elemental forces which shriek at mankind through the bars of his civilisation, like untamed beasts in a cage. Then he took the envelope itself, held it up to the light, and very carefully studied both the exterior and the flap. “It is Basilisk’s writing,” said he thoughtfully. “I can hardly doubt that it is Basilisk’s writing, though I have seen it only twice before. The Greek e with the peculiar top flourish is distinctive. But if it is Basilisk, then it must be something of the very first importance.” He was speaking to himself rather than to me; but my vexation disappeared in the interest which the words awakened. “Who then is Basilisk?” I asked. “Basilisk, Lovegood, is a nom-de-plume, a mere identification mark; but behind it lies a shifty and evasive personality. In a former letter he frankly informed me that the name was not his own, and defied me ever to trace him among the teeming millions of this great city. Basilisk is important, not for himself, but for the great man with whom he is in touch. Picture to yourself the pilot fish with the shark, the jackal with the lion—anything that is insignificant in companionship with what is formidable: not only formidable, Lovegood, but sinister—in the highest degree sinister. That is where he comes within my purview. You have heard me speak of Professor Order?” “The famous scientific criminal, as famous among crooks as—” “My blushes, Lovegood!” Ron murmured in a deprecating voice. “I was about to say, as he is unknown to the public.” “A touch! A distinct touch!” cried Ron. “You are developing a certain unexpected vein of pawky humour, Lovegood, against which I must learn to guard myself. But in calling Order a criminal you are uttering libel in the eyes of the law—and there lie the glory and the wonder of it!
